title: How do microservices maintain sessions when jumping between services (stateless JWT in the Authorization header, each service validates)?
shortTitle: How do microservices maintain sessions when jumping between services

s1_definition.profdef: Microservices generally do not maintain traditional server-side sessions; they use stateless authentication where the client carries a self-contained signed token, typically a JWT, in the `Authorization` header on every request, and each service independently validates the token's signature, expiry, issuer, and audience to establish the caller's identity and roles without any shared session store. Because the identity travels with the request and each service verifies it locally, any instance of any service can handle any request, which is what makes the architecture horizontally scalable and resilient.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh visits several departments at National Bank of India during one trip. In an old single-office system, the receptionist would keep a note saying "Rajesh is currently inside", and every clerk would phone the receptionist to confirm. That breaks when there are many branches. Instead the bank gives Rajesh a tamper-proof pass when he proves his identity, and he simply shows that pass at every department. Each department reads the pass and verifies the official stamp itself, with no phone call to anyone, so Rajesh can walk into any department in any branch and be recognized instantly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Microservices stay stateless by having the client carry a signed JWT in the Authorization header on every request, and each service validates it locally, so there is no shared session and any instance can serve any request.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Microservices generally do not maintain traditional server-side sessions; they use stateless authentication where the client carries a self-contained signed token, typically a JWT, in the `Authorization` header on every request, and each service independently validates the token's signature, expiry, issuer, and audience to establish the caller's identity and roles without any shared session store. Because the identity travels with the request and each service verifies it locally, any instance of any service can handle any request, which is what makes the architecture horizontally scalable and resilient.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh visits several departments at National Bank of India during one trip. In an old single-office system, the receptionist would keep a note saying "Rajesh is currently inside", and every clerk would phone the receptionist to confirm. That breaks when there are many branches. Instead the bank gives Rajesh a tamper-proof pass when he proves his identity, and he simply shows that pass at every department. Each department reads the pass and verifies the official stamp itself, with no phone call to anyone, so Rajesh can walk into any department in any branch and be recognized instantly.

**One line to remember:** Microservices stay stateless by having the client carry a signed JWT in the Authorization header on every request, and each service validates it locally, so there is no shared session and any instance can serve any request.

sections.s2_technical:
To understand why stateless tokens are used, recall the traditional model. A classic monolith creates a server-side session on login, stores it in memory, and hands the client a session id in a cookie; every request looks up that session to know who the user is. This works for one server, but in microservices you have many services and many instances of each, often behind a load balancer, so a session stored in one instance's memory is invisible to the others. The next request might land on a different instance that knows nothing about the session, breaking the login. You could share sessions in a central store like Redis, which some systems do, but that reintroduces a shared dependency on every request, adds latency, and becomes a scaling bottleneck and single point of failure.

The stateless JWT model removes the shared session entirely. On login an identity provider or auth service verifies credentials once and issues a signed JWT that itself contains the claims, the subject, the roles, the issuer, the audience, and the expiry. The client stores that token and sends it in the `Authorization: Bearer` header on every subsequent request. Each service, when it receives a request, validates the token locally: it checks the signature using the shared secret for HMAC or the public key for RSA, confirms the token has not expired, and verifies the issuer and audience. If all pass, the service reads the subject and roles straight from the token and proceeds, with no lookup anywhere.

The consequence is that the token is the session. There is no server-side session object; the state the server used to hold is now inside the signed token the client carries. This is what makes the architecture scale: any instance of any service can handle any request because everything it needs is in the token, so you can add or remove instances freely and a request can hop from the accounts service to the transfer service to the statements service, each validating the same token independently.

RSA signing is preferred in a multi-service setup because the auth service signs with a private key and every service verifies with the public key, so services can validate tokens without holding any secret that could mint tokens. Services often fetch the public keys from a JWKS endpoint and cache them, keyed by the key identifier in the token header so keys can rotate. The gateway may validate the token once at the edge too, but under zero trust each downstream service still validates it, so trust is never assumed from the network.

The honest tradeoff is revocation. Because a JWT is self-contained and validated locally, there is no central place to invalidate it, so a token remains valid until it expires even if the user logs out or is disabled. The standard mitigations are keeping access tokens short-lived, usually minutes, and pairing them with longer-lived refresh tokens that the client exchanges for new access tokens; logging out revokes the refresh token so no new access tokens can be minted, and the current access token simply expires shortly. For cases needing immediate revocation, you maintain a small denylist of revoked token identifiers, checked quickly, accepting that this adds a little shared state back for that specific need.

Senior nuances: never store sensitive data in the token because its payload is only encoded; always send tokens over TLS; validate audience so a token for one service is not replayed at another; propagate a correlation identifier for tracing across hops; and for the rare case where you truly need stateful server sessions, use a shared session store like Redis with sticky awareness, but understand you are trading scalability for immediate revocability.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs several instances of each service behind a load balancer, and Rajesh's requests land on different instances. With in-memory sessions he would be logged out randomly when a request hit an instance that did not have his session. This is exactly the stateless JWT case, where the token carries the identity so any instance recognizes him.

Problem 2 — During one logical operation Rajesh's request hops from the accounts service to the transfer service to the statements service. This is exactly the propagate-and-validate case, where each service independently validates the same token and reads his identity locally.

Problem 3 — The security team worried that a stolen token could be used indefinitely. This is exactly the revocation tradeoff, mitigated with short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens and an optional denylist.

Our mini-project demonstrates this. The code defines a `TokenIssuer` that mints a signed token on login, three services, `AccountService`, `TransferService`, and `StatementService`, that each independently validate the token, a `LoadBalancer` that routes each call to an arbitrary instance, and a demo that logs Rajesh in once and then hops across services and instances, all recognizing him from the same token, plus a short-lived token expiring to show the revocation model.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's login, after which he calls the accounts, transfer, and statement services in one trip, each call routed to an arbitrary instance.

Step 1: Rajesh logs in once. The token issuer verifies his credentials and mints a signed token carrying his subject, his CUSTOMER role, and an expiry. The client stores this token, and from now on it is the only thing that proves who he is.

Step 2: Rajesh calls the account service, and the load balancer routes it to some instance. That instance validates the token locally by checking the signature and expiry, reads his identity straight from the token, and serves the request with no session lookup.

Step 3: Rajesh then calls the transfer service, which the load balancer may route to a different instance entirely. It does not matter that this instance never saw him before, because it validates the same token independently and recognizes him instantly.

Step 4: Rajesh calls the statement service, again possibly on a fresh instance, and again it validates the same token and serves him. The identity hopped across three services and multiple instances purely through the token, with nothing shared on the server.

Step 5: To show the revocation model, a short-lived token is issued and then allowed to expire. When Rajesh presents the expired token, every service rejects it on the expiry check, and the client would then use its refresh token to obtain a new access token. The output shows the single login and each service recognizing him on arbitrary instances, then the expired token being rejected.

```
2026-10-24 15:06:14 INFO    Rajesh logged in once; token carries identity (no server session)
2026-10-24 15:06:14 INFO    [AccountService inst-2] rajesh (CUSTOMER) viewed SAV2001
2026-10-24 15:06:14 INFO    [TransferService inst-1] rajesh transfer to CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-24 15:06:14 INFO    [StatementService inst-3] rajesh statement last 30 days
2026-10-24 15:06:14 WARNING expired token rejected → client uses refresh token to get a new one
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Login (once)
    │ verify credentials
    ▼
  TokenIssuer.issue → signed JWT {sub, role, exp}  ← the "session" now lives in the token
    │ client stores token
    ▼
  Every request carries:  Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
    │
    ▼
  Load Balancer → ANY instance of ANY service
    │
    ├─▶ AccountService  inst-2  → validate(token) locally → serve
    ├─▶ TransferService inst-1  → validate(token) locally → serve
    └─▶ StatementService inst-3 → validate(token) locally → serve
         (no shared session store; each verifies signature + exp + iss + aud)

  Token expired? ──▶ rejected by ALL services ──▶ client exchanges refresh token for a new one
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Microservices generally do not maintain traditional server-side sessions at all; they use stateless authentication. On login an auth service verifies credentials once and issues a self-contained signed token, a JWT, that carries the claims: the subject, the roles, the issuer, the audience, and the expiry. The client stores that token and sends it in the Authorization bearer header on every request, and each service independently validates it by checking the signature, the expiry, the issuer, and the audience, then reads the identity straight from the token. The token is the session, so the state the server used to hold now lives inside the signed token the client carries.

The reason this matters is scalability. In a classic monolith you store a session in server memory and hand out a session id, which works for one server but breaks in microservices where there are many instances behind a load balancer, because a session in one instance's memory is invisible to the others, so the next request on a different instance would not recognize the user. You could share sessions in a central store like Redis, but that reintroduces a shared dependency on every request, adding latency and a scaling bottleneck. The stateless token removes that entirely: because everything needed is in the token and each service verifies it locally, any instance of any service can serve any request, so you add and remove instances freely and a request can hop from accounts to transfer to statements, each validating the same token independently.

In a multi-service setup I prefer RSA signing, where the auth service signs with a private key and every service verifies with the public key fetched from a JWKS endpoint and cached by key id, so services validate tokens without holding any secret that could mint them. The gateway may validate once at the edge, but under zero trust each downstream service still validates, so trust is never assumed from the network. The honest tradeoff I always mention is revocation: because a JWT is self-contained and validated locally, there is no central place to invalidate it, so it stays valid until it expires even after logout. I mitigate that by keeping access tokens short-lived, usually minutes, pairing them with longer-lived refresh tokens, so logout revokes the refresh token and the current access token simply expires shortly, and for cases needing instant revocation I keep a small denylist of revoked token ids.

On my project at National Bank of India we ran several instances of each service behind a load balancer, and stateless JWTs meant Rajesh logged in once and was recognized on any instance of the accounts, transfer, and statement services as his request hopped across them, with nothing shared on the server. When the security team worried about stolen tokens, we used five-minute access tokens with refresh-token rotation and a denylist for forced logout. The nuances I add are never storing sensitive data in the token because its payload is only encoded, always sending it over TLS, and validating the audience so a token for one service cannot be replayed at another.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that microservices stay stateless by having the client carry a signed JWT in the Authorization header on every request and each service validate it locally, so there is no shared session, any instance serves any request, and the only real tradeoff, revocation, is handled with short-lived access tokens, refresh tokens, and an optional denylist.

keyPoints: Database per service: each microservice owns its data
Idempotency: same request produces same result — safe retries
Eventual consistency: services sync via events, not distributed locks
Shared database anti-pattern: breaks service independence
